cards.title: Build landed unit cost and contribution per ecommerce order
cards.summary: Calculate product and delivery costs separately from advertising and overhead so pricing decisions use a consistent contribution measure.
cards.use_when: Pricing a product, deciding whether a SKU is viable, or setting up daily profit reporting in Shopify/Triple Whale.
steps: Start with net sales excluding pass-through taxes and recorded discounts/refunds.
Allocate inbound freight to units using a documented driver. A $11,000 container carrying 1,000 identical units adds $11 per unit, not $1.
Include manufacturing, applicable non-recoverable duties, inbound freight, pick/pack, outbound delivery, storage allocation and payment fees without double-counting.
Subtract advertising acquisition cost to calculate post-ad contribution; it is not net profit until remaining overhead and other expenses are considered.
Record landed product costs in the store/reporting system and reconcile fulfillment and advertising separately; verify the current integration.
Test the resulting contribution at plausible prices and acquisition costs before ordering; no single landed-cost-to-retail ratio guarantees viability.
caveats: Use current lane- and product-specific duty inputs from the responsible specialist, not blanket country assumptions.
This is a management contribution model; keep accounting classifications documented.

cards.title: Write a tech pack to control supplier quality and prove non-conformance
cards.summary: A tech pack documents drawings, fabric GSM, measurements, hardware, graphics and labels so manufacturing errors can be proven and disputed.
cards.use_when: Developing or re-sourcing any physical product, especially apparel, before placing a large purchase order.
steps: Include: (1) complete drawing with print placement, shape and colours; (2) fabric details — GSM/thickness, softness, colour references (strike-offs), and treatment specs like acid wash; (3) precise measurements for grading across S/M/L/XL; (4) graphics; (5) hardware (zips, pockets, closures); (6) labels and swing tags with company name and correct positioning — wrong or missing labels can trigger regional fines; and (7) packaging specs.

Keep physical reference samples of fabrics and strike-offs. When quality complaints arrive, cut a standard-size square of fabric and weigh it against the spec GSM to prove the supplier used thinner, wrong fabric — this is how Oodie resolved 'too thin' complaints and got replacements.
Use the tech pack to brief a second supplier for competitive quotes and to switch factories without redeveloping the product.
If needed, commission a tech-pack creator using a defined deliverable and current quote; the source's under-$200 price is anecdotal.
Retain the agreed tech pack, purchase order and supplier messages for quality disputes; platform protection is subject to current terms and does not guarantee a refund.
Any product has a tech pack; it just becomes more complex for injection-moulded or hardware-heavy goods.
caveats: The source's quality-improvement estimate is not a guarantee.
Document ownership, usage and exclusivity terms separately; neither the supplier nor the buyer automatically owns all IP merely because of this workflow.

cards.title: Negotiate MOQ, price and lead time as one trade-off set
cards.summary: Treat supplier MOQ, unit price and manufacturing lead time as the three levers to balance against cash flow and retail price.
cards.use_when: Selecting a supplier or placing a first or repeat purchase order.
steps: Obtain the supplier's actual minimum order quantity, unit price and manufacturing lead time; small custom runs may be possible at different economics.

Choose deliberately between higher price/lower MOQ (fits a small budget) and higher price/lower lead time (fits brands that want faster cash-flow turns). The source notes Oodie sometimes paid more for lower lead time.
Run the landed cost against your intended retail before committing. If landed cost forces a retail price that kills demand, do not launch that variant.

Write refund/tolerance terms into the supplier relationship before transferring large sums: what happens if product arrives different, tolerance for wrong quantities, and how you verify claimed quantities.
Resolve important specifications, ownership and remedies in agreed terms before committing funds; relationship-building does not establish these rights.
Compare multiple factories and consider de-speccing the product to hit a viable cost — the source estimates ~20% price improvement is achievable through comparison and negotiation.
caveats: MOQs, contract terms and savings depend on supplier and product; the source's 20% saving is an example, not a benchmark.

cards.title: Order against the outputs: operations as an input→process→output system
cards.summary: Model operations as inputs → processes → outputs, and judge every change by whether it improves the customer-facing output while cutting inputs and process load.
cards.use_when: Deciding which operational initiative to fund or fix (warehouse change, automation, forecasting hire) and how to justify it against marketing spend.
steps: Define the output as the customer experience, not an internal metric. A process improvement that doesn't change what the customer receives is not the goal.
Reduce inputs (cost) and process load (labour/steps) through automation and negotiation to get more output for less — this is the lens for every freight, 3PL and supplier decision.

Use the two-brand cost comparison to justify the work: if brand A lands product at $21 and brand B at $28 due to worse freight, courier, product and warehousing terms, brand A has ~$7 more per unit to spend on marketing — improving CAC headroom and profit.
Test this by comparing parallel supplier/3PL/freight quotes on freight (e.g. $5 vs $6), product ($10 vs $12), courier ($5 vs $8), storage ($1 vs $2).
Treat operations as weeding a garden: without consistent cadence, the sales/marketing 'plants' stop producing as much.
Assign ownership to a COO-type role once you can afford it; below roughly $1M revenue, the founder often holds all these roles.
caveats: The $21/$28 and 20% figures are illustrative example numbers from the source, not a standard.
Needs dedicated ops attention to realise — the source attributes missed growth to lacking an ops role during a demand spike.

cards.title: Build a critical path to hit launch and seasonal deadlines
cards.summary: A critical path sequences every product-development step with durations and dates so slips are visible and you avoid missing peak trading windows.
cards.use_when: Planning any product launch or seasonal buying cycle where missing a ship date means stranded inventory (e.g. Christmas).
steps: List every step: strike-offs/prints, first sample, revised sample, production sample, QC, bulk production, freight, and inbound to warehouse.
Sequence them in order and assign a duration to each (e.g. DHL sample from China ~5 days).

Set dates against each step from the target launch/ship date and use a project tool (Monday.com, Asana, Notion, Excel) with reminders for overdue tasks; on slip, push downstream dates or identify slack.
Assign an owner to each step and monitor daily. Don't let suppliers edit the critical path themselves — they can manipulate dates and you lose visibility.

Book a QC agent for the first, and ideally second/third, production run: they visit the factory, weigh and measure product against the tech pack and check Pantone colour. Alibaba has an inbuilt QC function; SGS also does compliance.
Work backwards from the Christmas shipping cut-off — failing to receive samples on time cascades to missing peak trade and leaves you holding stock through January/February.
caveats: Tooling changes; the specific apps named may differ in current interface.
QC via Alibaba or SGS incurs cost and lead time of its own.

cards.title: Forecast demand on an in-stock window, not a raw calendar period
cards.summary: Base forecasts on periods you were actually in stock and on comparable prior-year/month velocity, then apply a growth rate.
cards.use_when: Replenishment planning for any SKU before placing a purchase order.
steps: Never forecast from a period containing stockouts. If you were out of stock 15 days of a 30-day month, use the 15 in-stock days and extrapolate — the source notes forecast misses of 50% common when this is ignored.
If under ~1 year of history or growing fast, use month-on-month: e.g. 100→120→145→175 suggests ~20% growth and a linear-to-slightly-exponential projection for the next month.

Where seasonality dominates (most ecommerce due to Black Friday and holiday gifting), build a month-by-month curve: e.g. Jul 200, Aug 210, Sep 205, Oct 2,000, Nov 4,000, then a sharp drop after the Christmas shipping cut-off.
Find product-driven seasonality via Google Trends (e.g. 'beach tent' spikes in summer) and account for northern vs southern hemisphere opposites.
Apply a growth-rate assumption (e.g. 20–40% monthly) in your tool or Excel, then output two answers: sell-out date and replenishment quantity.
Review on a weekly, fortnightly or monthly cadence; picking the wrong comparison window is the top forecasting error.
caveats: Growth-rate figures are source examples, not targets.
Too much inventory ties up all profit and cash (existential risk); too little yields zero revenue against fixed costs.

cards.title: Set lead time, days-of-stock and safety stock inputs in the forecast tool
cards.summary: Feed supplier lead time, target days of stock and a small safety-stock buffer into the planner so sell-out and reorder-point outputs are realistic.
cards.use_when: Configuring replenishment thresholds and deciding how much working capital to commit to inventory.
steps: Enter supplier manufacturing lead time (e.g. 100 days) — longer lead times push the tool to trigger orders earlier.
Set target days of stock based on volatility and available capital: typical ranges are 4, 8 or 12 weeks.

Add 5–10 days safety stock as a buffer only after padding lead time with your average (rather than best-case) figure — the source says safety stock shouldn't really be needed if lead time is properly padded.
Use the tool output to get sell-out date and replenishment amount, then raise the purchase order.

Simple calculators (e.g. Inventory Planner, which the source recommends and uses; verify current features) or a custom Excel sheet both work — the goal is visibility on prior results to make future assumptions.
Consider hiring an ops manager (not necessarily a dedicated demand planner) to run this weekly once you're profitable and paying yourself.
caveats: Days-of-stock values are source heuristics that depend on industry, business age, volatility and cash.
Demand-planning tools exist (NetSuite, Walmart-grade systems); the source still ends up back at Excel for flexibility.

cards.title: Use purchase orders as the single cross-functional source of truth
cards.summary: A PO is more than an invoice — it must be visible to finance, ops, marketing and customer service so stock arrival and discontinuations are coordinated.
cards.use_when: Raising, landing or discontinuing any stock order, and coordinating teams around inbound inventory.
steps: Create a formal PO (product, price, quantities, ship-to, terms) rather than just an ad-hoc Alibaba order.
Route it to finance (for invoice payment), ops (for inbound stock timing), and marketing (so they time promotions to arrivals).
Flag discontinuations and near-landing POs to customer service so agents don't refund or promise products you can't supply.
Adopt an ERP once you're past roughly $30–50M revenue — the source says an ERP handles ~90% of these ops functions; below that a spreadsheet/PM tool can suffice.
Keep the PO as the reference in Alibaba Trade Assurance disputes alongside the tech pack.
caveats: The $30–50M ERP threshold is the source's heuristic.
Fragmented POs across Alibaba and internal tools are the common failure mode to avoid.

cards.title: Protect against 3PL failure with SLAs and multi-warehouse RFPs
cards.summary: Specify picked-on-time, delivered-on-time and cycle-count SLAs, and run a request-for-pricing across multiple warehouses to create competitive bids.
cards.use_when: Selecting or reviewing a 3PL, or negotiating fulfilment rates and service guarantees.
steps: Write a 3PL RFP ('Request for Pricing') that submits your volume forecasts and product dimensions to several warehouses so they bid competitively against each other.
Require in the SLA: picked-on-time guarantees, delivered-on-time tracking, and mandated bi-annual cycle counts.
Compare rates across providers for courier, pick-pack and storage, and factor these into unit economics.

Treat the 3PL as an existential dependency: the source describes a provider failing to ship during a forecast $45–50M October/November peak, causing promotions to be switched off, wrong products shipped and an estimated $20M+ in lost revenue.
Build trust and references — the source maintains a vetted list of ~10 3PLs and recommends introduction, noting the relationship is hard to get right.
Keep a contingency path (alternate 3PL, ability to switch) because a contracted underperformer is hard to fix mid-peak.
caveats: The $20M loss and $45–50M peak are the source's own case figures, not a benchmark.
The source discloses affiliate/relationship interests in its 3PL list.

cards.title: Keep import duties and collected sales taxes separate in the cost model
cards.summary: Use verified import-cost inputs and net-revenue reporting rather than treating all tax amounts as the same expense.
cards.use_when: Building landed cost for cross-border sourcing or setting up tax handling in the store backend.
steps: Obtain the applicable product classification, origin, destination and current duty/tax treatment from the responsible customs or tax specialist.
Add confirmed non-recoverable import costs to the model; do not infer zero duty from a country pair or trade agreement alone.
Separate taxes collected for remittance from net revenue, and identify recoverable versus non-recoverable amounts.
Configure store collection and reporting against the confirmed requirements; a generic tax checkbox is not a complete setup.
Reconcile the modeled amounts with actual invoices and settlements.
caveats: The source's country-level examples are not verified current rates or permissions.

cards.title: Choose supplier co-development vs independent product design
cards.summary: Compare supplier co-development with independently commissioned design on cost, control and documented rights.
cards.use_when: Committing to a product development route for a new or differentiated product.
steps: For supplier co-development, clarify existing designs, customization, reuse rights and what is included in the quote.
For independent design, commission clear deliverables and ownership/usage terms, then seek comparable manufacturing quotes using the tech pack.
Document tooling, design rights, confidentiality and exclusivity separately rather than assuming one development route guarantees ownership or defensibility.
Compare total development cost, lead time, manufacturability and customer demand before choosing.
caveats: Rights depend on agreements and applicable law; exclusivity and enforceability are not guaranteed by a tech pack.

cards.title: Run forecasting continuously to avoid the two existential inventory failures
cards.summary: Selling out or over-ordering are both business-ending risks; forecast so cash isn't trapped in inventory while peak is covered.
cards.use_when: Deciding SKU expansion and seasonal buy quantities under cash constraints.
steps: Recognise both failure modes: under-ordering yields $0 revenue against fixed costs; over-ordering ties up all profits in inventory so you can't acquire customers or pay taxes.
Expand SKUs cautiously — adding colour/size variants multiplies the forecast risk and capital requirement.

Note the retail baseline (big-box retailers work to ~5% forecast variance); fast-growing ecommerce misses by far more — the source cites 50% misses. Build for that uncertainty with days of stock and buffer rather than pretending to precision.
For very new products, forecast from comparable existing products and recent marketing performance as your best guest.

The source attributes much of Oodie's miss during the COVID-driven ecommerce surge — a forecast $45–50M peak period — to having no ops/planning role, estimating the business could have been 30–40% larger with one.
Set a review cadence (weekly/fortnightly/monthly) and assign an owner.
caveats: The 30–40% opportunity and 50% miss are the source's own estimates.
Retailer 5% variance is the industry baseline cited, not achievable for most ecommerce.
